shippingNews.postTitle: USS Silversides Back Home Following Historic Dry Dock Restoration

stories.body: MUSKEGON, MI – After more than three months away from its home port, one of the most decorated American submarines of World War II has made its way back across Lake Michigan. A crowd watches as the SIlversides returned to Muskeson Saturday morning. [Brian Caswell] The USS Silversides (SS-236), a 312-foot Gato-class submarine that has been a landmark along the Muskegon Channel since 1987, departed Sturgeon Bay, Wis., Friday afternoon following a $3.5 million preservation project at Fincantieri Bay Shipbuilding. shippingNews.postTitle: USS Silversides Returning Home to Muskegon

stories.body: Silversides tow. [North Shore Marine Terminal] STURGEON BAY, WI – The World War II-era submarine USS Silversides, which has been at Fincantieri Bay Shipbuilding in Sturgeon Bay for a major overhaul, left late Friday afternoon under tow headed back to her Muskegon home port. The submarine, which sank 23 enemy ships, underwent a $3.5 million preservation project to ensure its long-term stability. Doing tug work at the bow was Nickelena, built in 1973 for the US Navy, now works for Basic Marine Inc. At the stern was Erika Kobasic, built in 1939 for the US Coast Guard. Rosann Hollinger View a Face

shippingNews.postTitle: R/V Neil Armstrong Heads for Great Lakes

stories.body: The R/V Neil Armstrong departed its home port of Woods Hole, Massachusetts, on Wednesday, October 28. It will travel from Cape Cod down the St. Lawrence Seaway, through the locks, and across the Great Lakes. The 238-foot vessel is expected to arrive in Duluth on November 9. R/V Neil Armstrong is Great Lakes-bound. As of Thursday morning, the Neil Armstrong was traveling up the Atlantic Coast around Nova Scotia. todayInHistory.title: Sam Laud
todayInHistory.text: Sam Laud Bay Shipbuilding Corp. of Sturgeon Bay, WI, laid the keel for their hull # 712 on Jan. 4, 1974 to be built as a smaller-sized Great Lakes self-unloading bulk cargo carrier. The new vessel was launched on Nov. 19, 1974 for Buffalo's American Steamship Co. (ASC), a subsidiary of GATX Corp., Chicago, IL. Completed in 1975, the self-unloader was christened Sam Laud by Mrs. Edna Laud on behalf of her husband at a christening ceremony held April 15, 1975. Mr. Laud was the former president (1945) and chairman of the board (1956) of GATX Corp., having started with the company in 1916 as shop painter and riveter. Mr. Laud died August 1, 1963. GATX Corp. had acquired ASC in July of 1973. Mrs. Laud was accompanied by Mr. Frederick G. Jaicks, chairman and CEO of Inland Steel Co., Chicago, IL, who gave the address at the christening ceremonies. One of a new generation of self-unloaders for the ASC fleet, the Sam Laud was built at an approximate cost of $13.3 million and was the fourth of 10 self-unloaders launched for the fleet under Chapter XI of the Merchant Marine Act of 1970. Under this act, the U.S. government-guaranteed financing and tax deferred benefits for fleet modernizing. The other ASC self-unloaders built under this program were the Roger M. Kyes (now Adam E. Cornelius, 1973), Charles E. Wilson (now John J. Boland, 1973), H. Lee White (1974), St. Clair (1976), Belle River (now Walter J. marineWeather.synopsis: A 30.5 inch high pressure moving into the Eastern Seaboard later today continues to extend a 30.2 inch ridge over Lake Superior the rest of today into this evening. Monday, a 29.4 inch low lifts from Colorado into the Northern Plains, then heads towards the Upper Mississippi Valley at 29.6 inches Monday night and Tuesday. Pressure falls over Lake Superior from 30.1 inches Monday morning to 29.7 inches Tuesday morning. The Colorado low then slowly trudges eastward from southern Minnesota throughout Wednesday before arriving over Upper Michigan Wednesday night at 29.7 inches. Meanwhile, pressure over Lake Superior remains near 29.7 inches. Thursday into Friday, the low departs swiftly northeast toward Newfoundland while remaining at 29.7 inches and ridging to 30.0 inches builds in over Lake Superior.

High pressure near 30.5 inches will drift southeast into the northeastern United States through this afternoon, maintaining south-southeasterly winds over Lake Michigan. Low pressure near 29.5 inches will develop over eastern Colorado this evening, progressing into the Upper Mississippi River Valley by early Tuesday morning. Winds will steadily become gusty ahead of the low, approaching or exceeding gale force over at least the central third of the lake Tuesday afternoon and evening. Anticipate that headlines will become necessary in later forecasts. Rain will accompany the approaching/passing low Monday through Tuesday night, with a few thunderstorms possibly mixing in. Severe weather is not expected at this time. Winds will remain breezy, though likely below gale levels Wednesday and Wednesday night as 30.1 inch high pressure slowly builds into the Canadian Great Plains. Said high will move into the western Great Lakes through the second half of next week, allowing for westerly and eventually northerly winds by next weekend.

High pressure expands into the mid Atlantic today while increasing to 30.60 inches. This high will sustain relatively light winds. A slow moving deepening low pressure system will move from the central Plains Monday to northern Minnesota Tuesday. This system will drag a slow moving cold front into the Great Lakes region Tuesday night into Wednesday as the low lifts into northern Ontario.

High pressure 30.50 inches over New England will slowly shift east through Tuesday. A warm front will lift north across the lake late Tuesday into Wednesday before a cold front pushes east on Thursday.

A 30.5 inch high will settle over the northern Mid Atlantic states Sunday through Monday before drifting off the eastern seaboard Tuesday. A 29.5 inch low is then forecast to move very slowly from the upper Mississippi Valley Tuesday to the upper Great Lakes by Wednesday, and then into western Quebec by Thursday and Friday.
